prompt_free_text:
This paper studies a timely and interesting problem: how to obtain formal privacy guarantees for activation-steering-based alignment of LLMs. The core proposal, PSA, is simple: compute mean steering vectors from paired positive/negative demonstrations, clip per-example difference vectors, and add Gaussian noise so that the released steering vectors satisfy differential privacy. The paper also argues that once the private steering vectors are released, arbitrarily many downstream generations incur no further privacy cost by post-processing, and it supplements the formal guarantee with an empirical membership inference attack tailored to steering. Overall, I find the problem important and the high-level idea appealing. The work appears to be among the first to explicitly connect activation editing and differential privacy. At the same time, the current version has several technical ambiguities, some likely errors in the DP accounting and mechanism specification, and an empirical evaluation that is suggestive but not yet fully convincing by top-tier standards.

The main strength of the paper is conceptual novelty. Activation steering is increasingly used as a lightweight alignment mechanism, and it is reasonable to ask whether private demonstrations used to construct steering vectors can leak information. Framing the steering vector itself as the privatized object is elegant, because it naturally yields the “infinite-query” property through DP post-processing. This is a meaningful distinction from many inference-time privacy methods that spend privacy budget per query. The paper also does a good job motivating why activation editing may still leak information despite not updating model weights. The empirical section spans multiple behaviors and several open models, which helps demonstrate breadth.

I also appreciate the attempt to go beyond theorem statements and audit privacy empirically. The canary-based MIA is intuitive for this setting, where standard loss-based attacks are less natural. The observation that non-private steering can induce measurable membership leakage is useful in itself, even if the exact attack could be strengthened. The scaling discussion is also potentially interesting: if larger models are more robust to DP perturbations in steering space, that could matter practically.

That said, my biggest concern is the technical correctness and clarity of the DP mechanism. As written, Algorithm 1 appears inconsistent with the stated clipping operation and with standard Gaussian mechanism calibration. The algorithm defines
\bar d_i^l = d_i^l / max{C_l, ||d_i^l||_2}.
This ensures ||\bar d_i^l||_2 <= 1/C_l only if interpreted one way, or <= 1 if interpreted as standard clipping divided by max(C, norm); but the surrounding text says vectors are “projected to an L2 ball of radius C_l and then scaled by the same constant C_l,” which would indeed produce norm at most 1. The notation is therefore confusing, and the sensitivity calculation depends critically on it. If each processed vector has norm at most 1, then replacing one record changes the average by at most 2/n, which matches the stated sigma up to whether the Gaussian noise is isotropic in d dimensions. But if the clipping formula is not exactly standard, the sensitivity may differ. This needs to be stated rigorously and consistently.

Relatedly, the Gaussian mechanism is written as adding N(0, sigma^2), which is not dimensionally correct for a d-dimensional vector unless the authors mean isotropic Gaussian N(0, sigma^2 I_d). This is a small notation issue but important in a DP paper. More importantly, the privacy accounting across layers is simplistic and possibly misleading. The paper states that each layer-specific steering vector is made independently private with parameters (epsilon, delta), and then basic composition yields (|S| epsilon, |S| delta). That is fine as a worst-case bound if each layer uses the full dataset independently. However, the experimental section reports a fixed noise standard deviation of 0.02 and then derives per-layer and total epsilon values. It is not clear whether epsilon is chosen first and sigma derived from it, or sigma is fixed and epsilon back-computed. The latter is acceptable for reporting, but then the mechanism is not “parameterized by epsilon” in the usual sense. More importantly, because the same examples contribute to all selected layers, there may be opportunities for tighter accounting, but the paper does not explore them. That is not fatal, but the current presentation overstates rigor while leaving key details underspecified.

A second major concern is that the privacy guarantee is only as meaningful as the adjacency relation and the released object. The paper says neighboring datasets differ in one record, where a record is a full paired demonstration (p_i, c_i^+, c_i^-). That is reasonable, but it should be emphasized more clearly in the theorem statement. Also, the guarantee applies to the released steering vectors, not to the pretrained model itself. Since the base model may already memorize private information from pretraining, the end-to-end system is not globally private with respect to arbitrary user data; it is only private with respect to the alignment dataset used to compute the steering vectors. The paper mostly understands this, but some phrasing such as “ensures the generated texts for any query are differentially private” is too broad and could be misread. The guarantee is conditional on the fixed base model and only concerns the steering dataset.

The empirical evaluation is promising but incomplete. The paper compares PSA to mean steering, PCA steering, and zero-shot across seven behaviors and four models, which is good coverage. However, many important experimental details are missing or underdeveloped. It is unclear how the selected layers were chosen for each model and task, whether the same layers are used across all methods, whether hyperparameters such as clipping thresholds C_l and steering strength lambda were tuned on public validation data, and how sensitive results are to these choices. Since clipping thresholds directly affect both utility and privacy, they are central to the method, yet they are barely discussed. The paper says they “can either be optimised or estimated using a small public dataset,” but does not specify what was actually done in experiments. If thresholds were tuned on private data, that would consume privacy budget unless done carefully.

The utility results are also somewhat hard to assess without statistical uncertainty. Figure 3 is described qualitatively, but no confidence intervals or repeated-seed variability are reported. Since PSA injects random noise, variance across runs is essential. A single noisy draw can occasionally outperform the non-private baseline by chance, which the paper notes as “PSA sometimes improves on non-private steering.” Without repeated trials and error bars, it is difficult to know whether these differences are meaningful. This is especially important because the claimed privacy cost appears modest; one would like to see robustness over multiple noise realizations.

The text-generation evaluation using GPT-4 as judge is weakly informative in its current form. Only Llama-2-7B results are shown in Table 3, and the scores are often extremely close across methods, sometimes also close to zero-shot. It is not clear what exact rubric GPT-4 used, whether pairwise or absolute scoring was employed, whether order effects were controlled, or whether human validation was performed. Table 4, intended as a qualitative example, is not persuasive: both outputs appear to continue a hallucinated premise rather than resist it, which raises questions about whether the “hallucination” steering is actually improving factuality in open-ended generation. More broadly, the multiple-choice behavioral benchmarks are inherited from prior work, but they are narrow proxies for alignment. The paper would be stronger with at least one more realistic open-ended evaluation per behavior, or a clearer explanation of what these benchmarks do and do not measure.

The MMLU section is useful in spirit but currently undercut by presentation issues. Table 5 appears incomplete or malformed: the zero-shot row is truncated, and one cell is blank. This makes it hard to verify the claim that zero-shot performance remains the same in all settings. More generally, evaluating “general capabilities” by converting MMLU to A/B format may not be very sensitive, and again no uncertainty is reported. Since steering is applied at every token and selected layer during generation, one might also worry about effects on calibration, verbosity, or refusal behavior outside the target domain; these are not examined.

The empirical privacy evaluation is one of the more interesting parts, but it also has limitations. The canary-based MIA is tailored and intuitive, yet it is a fairly narrow attack that depends on synthetic anchor-target associations and repeated sampling at temperature 0.8. It demonstrates one leakage channel, not necessarily overall privacy risk. The threshold tau is chosen differently for different models, but the selection procedure is not justified. Was tau tuned on held-out attack data? If so, how much attack-side information is assumed? Also, the attack is only evaluated on the hallucination dataset and two models. It would be more convincing to test across multiple behaviors and to compare against stronger baselines, such as attacks using logprobs if available, nearest-neighbor decoding patterns, or prompt variations around the anchor. The reported empirical epsilon values are interesting, but readers should be reminded that empirical epsilon from a specific attack is only a lower bound on worst-case privacy leakage, not a substitute for formal DP. The paper gestures at this but could be more careful.

There are also several writing and presentation issues that detract from confidence. Equation 2 appears to be missing and replaced by unrelated text (“Significant improvement in performance is shown by the results. We find that the model adapts well across different languages.”), which looks like an editing artifact. Algorithm 1 contains a likely typo in d_i^l = h_l((p,c^+)) - h_l((p_i,c_i^-)); the first term seems to omit the index i. The dataset definition uses indices from i=0 to n in one place and i=1 to n elsewhere. The paper says it evaluates “three state-of-the-art LLMs” in the contributions but later uses four models. There are multiple grammatical issues and malformed footnotes. For a paper making formal privacy claims, these inconsistencies matter because they make it harder to trust the exact mechanism.

I think the paper would be substantially stronger with the following revisions. First, clean up the formalism: define the clipping operator precisely, state the sensitivity proof explicitly, specify the Gaussian as N(0, sigma^2 I_d), and provide a theorem with assumptions and adjacency relation. Second, clarify the experimental protocol for choosing layers, thresholds C_l, and lambda, and ensure any tuning on private data is either avoided or privacy-accounted. Third, report mean and standard deviation over multiple PSA noise draws and, ideally, multiple decoding seeds. Fourth, add stronger ablations on privacy-utility tradeoffs by varying sigma or epsilon directly, rather than fixing sigma=0.02 and reporting resulting epsilons. Fifth, strengthen the privacy audit with more attack variants and more tasks. Sixth, fix the presentation issues, especially the missing equation and malformed tables.

A few more technical questions deserve attention. Why privatize only mean steering and not PCA steering? PCA on private data is itself a nontrivial DP problem; perhaps that is why it is omitted, but the paper should say so explicitly rather than simply using PCA as a non-private baseline. Also, because the steering vector is added at every token position, the effective perturbation to generation may be much larger than the perturbation to the vector itself; some discussion of how lambda interacts with DP noise would be useful. Finally, the claim that larger models have a better privacy-utility tradeoff is plausible, but the current evidence is limited to one model family and one behavior. I would treat this as an observation rather than a general scaling law unless more evidence is added.

In summary, I like the problem and the basic idea. The paper opens a worthwhile direction at the intersection of activation engineering and privacy, and the “offline privatize the steering vector, then answer unlimited queries” framing is elegant and practically relevant. However, the current version falls short on technical precision and empirical rigor. My overall assessment is positive on novelty and potential impact, but cautious on correctness and completeness. With a careful revision addressing the DP mechanism details, stronger uncertainty reporting, and a more robust privacy evaluation, this could become a solid contribution. As it stands, I would view it as borderline for a top-tier venue.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces PSA, a differentially private activation-steering method for LLM alignment. The method computes per-layer steering vectors from paired positive/negative demonstrations, clips the per-example activation differences, adds Gaussian noise to the averaged vector, and then uses the privatized vectors during inference-time activation editing. The authors claim formal DP guarantees for infinitely many downstream queries via post-processing, and empirically evaluate PSA on seven alignment-related behaviors across several open LLMs. They report that PSA often matches non-private mean steering while outperforming zero-shot baselines, has limited impact on MMLU, and reduces success of a proposed canary-based membership inference attack.
strengths: Timely and relevant problem: privacy-preserving alignment with private demonstrations is important and underexplored, especially for inference-time steering methods.
Conceptually simple approach: clipping plus Gaussian noise on steering vectors is easy to understand and implement.

The paper connects activation steering with differential privacy in a clean way and correctly leverages the intuition that once a privatized steering vector is released, unlimited downstream use is post-processing.
Broad empirical scope in terms of behaviors and multiple model families/sizes.
The paper includes an empirical privacy audit via a tailored canary-based membership inference attack, which is a useful addition beyond formal DP claims.
The utility goal is realistic: preserve most of the benefit of non-private steering rather than outperform it.
weaknesses: The DP mechanism and its presentation are mathematically imprecise in several places, weakening confidence in the formal guarantee as stated.

Algorithm 1 appears to contain a scaling/clipping error: the formula divides by max{C_l, ||d_i^l||_2}, which bounds norms by 1/C_l or 1 depending on interpretation, while the text says vectors are projected to an L2 ball of radius C_l and then scaled by the same constant. The intended sensitivity analysis is therefore unclear.
The Gaussian noise notation is dimensionally ambiguous: adding N(0, sigma^2) to a vector should specify a multivariate Gaussian N(0, sigma^2 I_d).

The sensitivity constant used in sigma seems under-justified. The paper uses sigma = 2*sqrt(2 ln(1.25/delta)) / (n epsilon), but this depends on the exact clipping convention; given the apparent clipping inconsistency, the proof sketch is incomplete.

Privacy accounting across layers is simplistic and potentially suboptimal; more importantly, the paper does not clearly define whether epsilon in Algorithm 1 is per-layer or global, which creates ambiguity between Table 2 and the theorem statement.

Empirical evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, variance across random noise draws, or significance testing are reported, despite stochastic privatization being central to the method.
The qualitative evaluation relies on GPT-4-as-judge without human validation, and the reported scores in Table 3 are difficult to interpret because many are extremely low and close across methods.
The MMLU table appears incomplete/corrupted, making the general-capability claim hard to verify from the presented evidence.
The privacy attack is narrow and synthetic, relying on inserted canaries and thresholded generations; it does not establish robustness against stronger or more realistic extraction attacks.
Comparison is limited mostly to privatized mean steering; there is no serious baseline against alternative private mechanisms or private prompt/ICL methods adapted to the same setting.
methodological_flaws: There is a likely mathematical error in the clipping definition. Standard clipping to radius C should be d_i * min(1, C/||d_i||) or equivalently d_i / max(1, ||d_i||/C). The paper instead uses d_i / max(C, ||d_i||), which is not equivalent unless C=1 and contradicts the textual description. This directly affects sensitivity and the claimed DP calibration.

Because the clipping formula is inconsistent, the stated sensitivity bound of 2/n and resulting Gaussian noise scale are not rigorously established. The formal DP guarantee may still be salvageable with corrected clipping, but as written the proof logic is incomplete.

The paper cites the classic Gaussian mechanism formula from older approximate-DP analyses, but does not carefully state assumptions or whether neighboring datasets differ by add/remove or replace-one semantics. This matters for the factor of 2 in sensitivity.

Equation 2, which should define how steering is applied to activations, is missing from the paper body and replaced by unrelated text ('Significant improvement...' etc.). This omission makes the method specification incomplete.

The empirical privacy evaluation computes an 'empirical epsilon' from FPR/FNR of one specific attack. This quantity is not a valid estimate of the true DP epsilon of the mechanism; at best it is an attack-dependent lower bound on distinguishability. The discussion risks overstating what empirical epsilon means scientifically.

The attack threshold tau is hand-chosen differently per model, but there is no principled calibration protocol or held-out tuning description. This can bias the reported attack success and weakens empirical validity.

The experiments fix a noise standard deviation of 0.02 while also discussing theoretical epsilon values. It is not fully clear whether all reported utility results correspond exactly to the DP-calibrated sigma implied by dataset size and epsilon, or whether sigma was manually chosen and epsilon back-computed. This ambiguity affects reproducibility and validity of the privacy-utility tradeoff claims.

Claims about scaling behavior are based on a limited slice (apparently one dataset/model family) and are partly speculative; no controlled analysis isolates whether improved tradeoff comes from model size, baseline alignment strength, or dataset/task specifics.
